items.headline: Global tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to AI slowdown fears
items.blurb: Investors have reacted to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry.
items.text: Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025. The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide. items.text: Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow to discuss regional security as diplomatic efforts gather pace to end the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. items.headline: Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office
items.blurb: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
items.text: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office. Trump, a former real estate mogul, has drastically altered the look of the president's official office during his second term, most notably with adding many gold features. "We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday. American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress. The executive order, which Trump signed on Thursday, declares the Oval Office to be a national monument, along with some of its surrounding rooms. The document also says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character". items.blurb: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling…
items.text: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure. The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections . In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. items.headline: White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
items.blurb: The Trump administration has downplayed reports the pair could be on their way out after heavy Republicans election losses.
items.text: The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration. US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses. One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort. "You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down." Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run. Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview. "I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'"

items.headline: California governor commutes sentences of more than 500 people on death row
items.blurb: Gavin Newsom cites state values and flaws in the legal system as he grants largest mass clemency in US history.
items.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom has announced that he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, the largest mass clemency in United States history. The announcement on Thursday effectively clears out California’s death row , although the state has not executed a prisoner for 20 years. Those on death row will instead serve life sentences without the possibility of parole. “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in an open letter. Support for the death penalty in the US has largely declined since the 1990s, although it still holds majority backing. A Pew Research Center poll released in August found that 66 percent of Americans supported the punishment for those convicted of murder. Roughly 73 percent, however, acknowledged there was a risk of executing an innocent person. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. items.headline: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
items.blurb: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
items.text: Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years. The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition". It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread. At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes". items.headline: Diktats, boycotts and the fight for rights
items.blurb: For over two years, 45 toddy-tapper and 10 Dalit families in Nizamabad’s Tallarampur have allegedly faced a complete social boycott for defying their Village Development Committee’s (VDC) orders. Denied access to groceries, medical aid and social gatherings, they have been pushed to the margins of everyday life.
items.text: Residents of different villages at a public hearing held by Telangana State Commission for Backward Classes, in Nizamabad last month. Nearly 90 complaints concerning alleged excesses by village development committees were put forth. | Photo Credit: Nagara Gopal On a sunny afternoon last year, 40-year-old Kairi Kalyani dressed in her festive best and stepped out of her home with a plate of offerings, including turmeric, kumkum , flowers, coconuts and fruits. It was Sri Rama Navami, and Kalyani, along with a dozen other women from her neighbourhood in Tallarampur village of Nizamabad district, arrived at the local Ramalayam to perform kumkumarchana . But what was meant to be a day of prayer and celebration quickly turned into an experience of humiliation. Just as the women settled among the other devotees, the temple priest allegedly asked them to leave. The reason? They belonged to the Goud (toddy-tapper) community and were not permitted to perform rituals at the temple! items.headline: How UGC’s equity rules evolved and why their contentious definitions are back under review
items.blurb: The Union government told the Supreme Court that it was considering setting up a panel to reconsider the framework
items.text: The University Grants Commission’s (UGC) 2026 equity regulations, now at the centre of a legal dispute over their definition of caste-based discrimination, followed a nearly seven-year legal battle and a year-long exercise involving an expert committee, stakeholder consultations and suggestions from petitioners seeking stronger safeguards against discrimination in higher education institutions. On Thursday, the Union government told the Supreme Court that it was considering setting up a committee to reconsider the framework, and was examining the issue to ensure that “no section feels dissatisfied or apprehensive”. The development comes over nine months after the court stayed the regulations, saying some provisions were “vague and could be misused”. The process began with a January 3, 2025, Supreme Court order directing the UGC to frame fresh regulations within six weeks in petitions filed in 2019 by Radhika Vemula and Abeda Salim Tadvi, the mothers of Rohith Vemula and Payal Tadvi. items.blurb: The package includes 130 crore reserved for primitive tribes, ₹30 crore reserved for the Pardhi community, and also provides for 100% government grant for individual and collective benefit schemes
items.text: Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis speaks during a meeting with the advisory committee for ‘Viksit Maharashtra 2047 ’ at Sahyadri Guest House in Mumbai. File | Photo Credit: ANI Under ‘Viksit Maharashtra 2047’, the Maharashtra Government made provision for a special package of ₹160 crore in the 2026–27 Budget for the “holistic development of the primitive tribes” — Katkari, Kolam and Madia — along with the Pardhi community. The package includes 130 crore reserved for primitive tribes, ₹30 crore reserved for the Pardhi community, and also provides for 100% government grant for individual and collective benefit schemes. The ₹130 crore will be further divided and allocated as follows: ₹100 crore for basic amenities and ₹30 crore for individual and collective benefit schemes. For the Pardhi community, ₹10 crore will be allocated for basic amenities and ₹20 crore for individual and collective benefit schemes. The announcement to provide funds through a special package for the holistic development of primitive communities was made in the 2026–27 Budget. items.headline: Supreme Court acquits school officials in Maharashtra tribal girl’s death in 2020 pillar collapse
items.blurb: The Bench said the school administrators could not be held criminally responsible merely for failing to ensure the pillar was properly constructed.
items.text: The Supreme Court has acquitted the president and hostel superintendent of a Maharashtra tribal residential school of culpable homicide charges over the death of a 12-year-old girl who was crushed when a poorly constructed pillar collapsed on her in 2020. In a judgment released on Thursday, the court held that a mere breach of duty or failure to ensure proper construction was insufficient to establish criminal liability in the absence of requisite knowledge or proof of gross negligence. A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan said the school administrators could not be held criminally responsible merely for failing to ensure proper construction of the pillar, particularly when the actual construction work had been entrusted to a contractor. “The mere failure to attain the standard of care prescribed by the law, thereby committing breach of such duty as observed by the high court would not be a criminal act,” noted the bench, setting aside the Bombay High Court’s February 2026 order refusing to quash the criminal proceedings against the two school officials. items.headline: Danger in the sewer: On India’s sewer cleaning deaths
items.blurb: India must eliminate situations that lead to sewer cleaning deaths
items.text: Despite legislation, Supreme Court orders, government programmes, the availability of mechanised cleaning technologies, and exhortations from politicians, India continues to lose sanitation workers to foreseeable, and largely preventable, circumstances. In a recent incident, four workers lost their lives in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh , cleaning a hotel’s food-waste chamber. According to Parliament and the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis data, the number of workers who died on jobs involving sewer and septic tanks was 859 between 2014 and 2025, 498 from 2019 to mid-2026, 332 across 18 States and Union Territories in 2021–26, and 1,350 between 1993 and 2025. The figures have never tended towards zero even as the Safai Karamchari Andolan has repeatedly alleged severe under-reporting. Further, the government has maintained since at least 2021 that the practice of manually cleaning excreta from insanitary latrines has been eliminated, effectively signalling that it believes it has addressed the root of the problem when it has not, and freeing administrative bodies of the urgency of inspecting municipalities and private establishments. items.text: The Delhi Traffic Police has put in place special traffic arrangements on roads around Anand Vihar inter-state bus terminal (ISBT) and adjoining transport hubs from November 5 to 15 to manage the anticipated surge in passenger movement during the festive season, two senior police officers said. Additionally, the traffic police have also issued an advisory, warning the public about the possible traffic commotion likely to be caused by heavy movement of passengers and informing them about the restrictions and diversions implemented on the roads. According to the advisory, two arterial roads – Chaudhary Charan Singh Marg (also known as Road No-56), connecting Dilshad Garden with Ghazipur roundabout, and Swami Dayanand Marg (Road No-57), connecting the Ghazipur flyover with Shahdara flyover via Jagatpuri and Hasanpur Depot – are likely to remain affected due to the festive rush at the transport hubs around the Anand Vihar. The company had posted a net profit of Rs 655.06 crore in the July-September quarter a year ago, according to a regulatory filing from Britannia Industries. Its revenue from operations was up 15.64 per cent to Rs 5,597.79 crore in the second quarter of FY27. It was at Rs 4,840.63 crore in the corresponding quarter. items.blurb: Anthropic IPO: Three major investors who plan to take part in the offering told a US media outlet that the valuation would likely need to be lowered, with one saying it could end up closer to $1 trillion.
items.text: Anthropic may have to accept a lower valuation than the $1.5 trillion it had been targeting for its stock market debut, after a sharp tech sell-off spooked key investors, the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. The development comes as rival OpenAI has delayed its plans to trade on Wall Street until next year, and companies in the Nasdaq composite lost $2.5 trillion in market value on Thursday as investors pulled back from AI bets. The artificial intelligence company is aiming to hold its initial public offering the week of November 16 and had been expected to raise up to $100 billion, which would make it the largest IPO on record. However, three major investors who plan to take part in the offering told the Journal the valuation would likely need to be lowered, with one saying it could end up closer to $1 trillion. Previous estimates had put the valuation at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. Anthropic's listing had been expected to surpass the record set by SpaceX's IPO in June, which raised $86 billion. They believe the recent correction has improved entry valuations for long-term investors, although traders should remain cautious about short-term price movements. items.text: It seems Elon Musk's political bet on Republican candidates, especially in Texas, in the US midterm elections has failed to deliver the outcome he may have hoped for. The shares of his companies have tumbled spectacularly in the last two trading sessions, losing $456 billion since Tuesday's close. With Democrats flipping several Republican held seats to take control of both chambers of Congress and winning the governor race in Texas, investors are increasingly concerned that Tesla and SpaceX could face tougher regulatory scrutiny, particularly over their ambitious artificial intelligence (AI) and data-centre expansion plans in the state, according to a report by CNBC . Tesla shares fell more than 11% on Thursday, while SpaceX shares declined nearly 9%. By the end of the session, the combined market capitalisation losses for the two companies had reached about $456 billion since Tuesday's close. Democratic victories in Texas have raised investor concerns about tougher oversight of data centres and AI infrastructure. New rules could delay projects or increase their costs. The startup has also inaugurated Base 1, a private facility dedicated to space debris removal and satellite servicing. The facility is designed to support the development of technologies for in-orbit repairs, refuelling and the recovery of defunct satellites. According to the company, Base 1 is the world’s sixth facility equipped with space vision effects and microgravity simulation capabilities. It brings together infrastructure for designing, building, testing and operating technologies required for satellite servicing and space debris recovery. Cosmoserve currently sources nearly 60% of its mission components locally. items.headline: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage

The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep.
items.text: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. items.text: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. items.text: Biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons The fresh capital will be used to expand ‘Venom Atlas’, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and strengthen its AI and laboratory screening capabilities The startup combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to identify and develop venom-derived molecules into potential therapeutic leads Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. The startup, spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to identify and develop venom-derived molecules into potential therapeutic leads. The fresh capital will be used to expand ‘Venom Atlas’, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and strengthen its AI and laboratory screening capabilities. The startup also plans to expand its team across venom biology, computational science and drug discovery, while supporting the validation and optimisation of promising molecules. items.headline: Sarvam’s Prism Enters India’s Growing AI Decision Model Race
items.blurb: AI models are increasingly being built to do more than answer questions. Some are now designed to make specific decisions,…
items.text: Sarvam AI has launched Prism, an open-weight decision model built on its Sarvam 105B model for fast, structured decisions across enterprise workflows. The launch puts Sarvam alongside Indian builders such as ConvAI Innovations and PurpleTalk’s Sthānika, as well as global players developing models designed to make decisions rather than generate text. Sarvam claims Prism achieves an average score of 71.8 across three evaluation indices, with a median response time of 44 milliseconds on an Nvidia B200 GPU. AI models are increasingly being built to do more than answer questions. Some are now designed to make specific decisions, such as whether a customer query should go to a sales or support team, whether a document needs further review, or whether an AI agent has completed a task correctly. In India, Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations was one of the first to explore this category with Laya, an open-weight decision model intended to run locally on devices such as laptops and phones.
